Agrawal, Carey and Livny 1987: blocking won for medium to high levels of resource utilization, and a restart-based method won only if utilization is low enough and many transactions are available (quoted l.1195-1197).
Agrawal, Carey and Livny 1987: 'the proper algorithm choice is strongly resource dependent' (quoted l.1197); the file reads the crossover as a resource level, not a conflict rate.
Agrawal, Carey and Livny 1987: 'the level of multiprogramming ... should be carefully controlled' (quoted l.1201-1203).
Kung and Robinson: 'in an optimistic approach, the major difficulty is starvation, which can be solved by using locking' (quoted l.214, lit1 #4).
Version control is optimistic control: a private copy, a validation and a publish (Kung, quoted l.58-59, lit1 #4).
Ports and Grittner: 'two concurrent transactions that read the same data, but modify disjoint sets of data' can break an invariant together (snapshot write skew; quoted l.36-55, lit1 #7).
Serializable snapshot isolation has a 'dangerous structure' (Ports, quoted l.162-166, lit1 #8).
Calvin needs advance knowledge of all transactions' read and write sets; a transaction that must read to learn them is restarted if its reconnoitered set is no longer valid (lit1 #9, quoted l.120).
Ordering before execution was 'the only protocol to maintain good performance despite high skew' (Harding, lit1 B3, quoted l.205-206).
Harding: throughput of a partitioned store fell 12-40 % from two to four partitions (lit1 B3, quoted l.296).
Silo: a partitioned store fell below optimistic control at about 20 % cross-partition transactions (lit1 B4, quoted l.434-436).
CALM: 'a program has a consistent, coordination-free distributed implementation if and only if it is monotonic' (lit3 #9, quoted p3 L119).
Invariant confluence: sequential order-ID numbering is the case that needs coordination ('order IDs should be assigned sequentially', lit3 #10, quoted p8 L439).
Invariant confluence: 'if invariants are incorrectly or incompletely specified, an I-confluent database system may violate application-level correctness' (lit3 #10, quoted p6 L291).
Scalable commutativity rule: changing an interface (an O_ANYFD flag; inode numbers from a per-core counter) makes operations commute (lit3 #1, quoted p14 L486, p13 L454).

Three-way merge: a clean merge is guaranteed only when the untouched middle holds a line occurring exactly once in each of O, A and B, and only for two edited regions; generalised, 'this generalization no longer ensures a conflict-free synchronization' (lit3 #14, quoted p7 L118-119, p9 L131).
Semistructured merge (Apel): fewer conflicts in 60 % of scenarios, by 34±21 %, but more conflicts in 26 % of them, by 109±170 % (lit3 #16, quoted p7 L462, p8 L569).
Structured merge: 39 % of the conflicts of line merge (lit3 #17, quoted p7 L332).
Cavalcanti 2017: the improved structured merge still had 20.60 % added false negatives (clean merges that are wrong), against 9.62 % for line merge (quoted p16 L211).
Imine: 'It is well known that these transformation functions are not correct' for published string transforms of operational transformation (lit3 #6, quoted p6 L77).
Boucheneb: 'if the number of sites exceeds 2 then the convergence property is not satisfied for all OT algorithms considered here' (lit3 #6, quoted abstract).
Uber 2019 (UBER19): testing every combination of waiting fixes gave P50 'up to 15x' of the ideal, and 'speculating deep instead of going wide helps' (lit5 #6, quoted l.1158-1163).
Uber 2019 SubmitQueue: up to 2.98x the ideal at P50 and 1.2x with 500 workers (lit5 #6, quoted l.1146-1156).
Uber 2019: a plain serial queue at 500 changes an hour gave turnaround of '80x, 129x and 132x' the ideal and a '95% slowdown' (lit5 #6, quoted l.1166-1167, l.1391).

Uber 2019 conflict analyser: up to 60 % better than the ideal's turnaround but only 20 % for the practical queue, because 'the build graph on the iOS monorepo is very deep' (lit5 #6, quoted l.1409-1418).
Uber (a model figure, lit5 #6, quoted l.243-244): a change 1 to 10 h stale makes mainline red at a rate of 10 to 20 %.
Uber 2025: per monorepo CPU cut 35 to 52 % and p95 wait cut 32 to 45 % against the 2019 queue by predicting build times (headline 53 %, 44 %, 37 %; lit5 #7, quoted l.144-145, l.1010-1082).
Ekstazi (EKS15): file-level test selection cut test time 32 % on average and 54 % for longer suites, but took up to 138 % of the full run on short suites (quoted l.21-26, l.827-832; lit5 #13).
Predictive test selection needs 'past three months' of outcomes (lit5 #12, quoted l.532-533).
Test files run side by side need tests that share no files or ports (lit5 #14, summary).
Google (TAP17): of 115,160 test targets that both passed and failed, 46,694 were flakes (40.5 %) (quoted l.441-445); the file reads this as about 60 % real breaks.
Predictions trained on flaky test results give 'very poor predictions' (lit5 #12, quoted l.121-124).
Flaky test failures mislead bisection (lit5 #8, summary).
Brun 2013: textual conflicts in merges by people, 16 % (quoted BRU13 l.504-515; lit5 #17).
Brun 2013: build or test conflicts of all merges, 1 % + 6 % = 7 % (quoted BRU13 l.504-515; lit5 #17).
Brun 2013's text says '33 percent of the 399 clean textual merges led to build or test conflicts', which the file says does not agree with its 1 % + 6 % (lit5 #17, corrections).
Brun 2013: conflicts between long-lived branches persisted 3.2 days (quoted BRU13 l.1796).
Kasi 2013: textual conflicts in merges by people, 7.6 to 19.3 % (quoted KAS13 l.49-52; lit5 #17).
Kasi 2013: build failures of 2.1 to 14.7 % and then test failures of 5.6 to 35 % of good builds (quoted l.49-52); the file's arithmetic gives 7.6 % to 44.6 % of clean merges failing.
Co-active AI-agent pull-request pairs: textual conflicts of 19.8 to 41.7 %, and 27.67 % in a second study (litA t9, summary).
Parallel agents: semantic conflicts of 5 to 10 % (litA t9, summary).
Passes alone but fails together: 1 of 834 mined pairs, and 97 % of constructed tasks (litA t9, summary).
Telling an agent of the other change recovered 82 % of runs (litA t9, summary, constructed tasks).
Greedy scheduling (paper tagged bl99): any greedy schedule finishes within T1/P + T_inf, 'universally optimal to within a factor of 2' (lit4 #2, quoted bl99 L316-323).
Graham (paper tagged graham66): critical-path-first is not near optimal with precedence, its best bound stays near 2; with no precedence it is '4/3 - 1/(3n)' (lit4 #5, quoted L735-779).
'An increase in the number of processing units can cause an increase in the total length of time' (lit4 #6, quoted L7-10).
In simulation, ratios of 1.1 or more over the best schedule 'are quite common' (lit4 #5, quoted L784-787).
The Universal Scalability Law C(N) = N / (1 + a(N - 1) + b N(N - 1)) and its peak N* = sqrt((1 - a)/b) are confirmed (lit4 #9, quoted eq. 5-6).
The USL peak formula reproduces three measured memcached fits with peaks 6.6 to 6.8 (lit4 #9b, quoted L560-583).
Gunther's own method asks for 'at least half a dozen data points' (quoted L108-126).
In one USL case a prediction from early data put the peak at 12,000 threads where measurement gave 2,000, a factor of 6 (quoted L707-712).
Group commit: 'flush the instant the device is free' came within about 0.1 % of the best tuned timer (lit4 #13, quoted L12-19; a 2026 preprint, one measured case).
Pipelining hides the check only while the gate's load rho is below 1 (lit4 #14, textbook; not fetched).
Zuul's window (lit5 #4, summary) is cited in the file as growing by one per clean merge and halving after a failed one.
Lock splitting, 'partition spacetime' (perfbook, lit2 #3, quoted l.5808).
Lock striping's 'almost n times' speed-up figure is a summary only; no open measured study of striping was found (litA t7, summary).
Bayou: a merge procedure per write (lit3 #12, summary).
Socio-technical congruence: 25 projects showed 'no statistical relationship' with bugs (lit5 #18, quoted STC21 l.15-16).
Sequence CRDTs for real-time co-editing show interleaving anomalies and growing metadata (lit3 #3 quoted p41 L1949; #4 and #5 are summaries).
Chosen order: 0b first, then one skeleton change, then 7 fixes at once (OUT, CLAIM, CGATE, REDO, W1, W6, W7) and the other 6 in three steps; without the skeleton only 4 could start at once.
The number of fixes running at once grows by one per clean merge and halves after a failed one.
The single suite check keeps up with the builders only while builders < (minutes to write one fix) / 10.
With the skeleton, textual merge conflicts should be near 0; this is not proven.
Expect 1 to 6 of the 13 clean merges to fail the tests, possibly more, since the fixes share 17 places by design (not measured).
Checking several ready fixes in one suite run pays while fewer than about 29 % of merges fail (2 to 4 per run).
A batch of k fixes saves suite runs when (1 - p)^k > 1/k, with a failed batch retested singly: p below 0.29 for k = 2 or 4, below 0.24 for k = 7.
Testing k fixes ahead of the queue: the chance all pass is (1 - p)^k, 0.75 for p = 0.07 and k = 4, 0.095 for p = 0.446; speculation gains time only at the low end of p.
A conflict analysis could separate only the 5 fixes that do not touch lib (CGATE, CLOSE, REDO, W4, W5).
Test selection is the builder's own pre-check (its test file and those of the scripts it touched); the gate runs the full suite, because a lib change selects every test file.
No retry on the merged tip; a failing test file is run once on the base without the fix: failing there means pre-existing or flaky, passing there means the fix broke it.
Side-by-side test files cannot finish faster than the longest file (270 s), so at most 596 / 270 = 2.2 times faster unless the selftest file is split.
Writing is locked by plan (one writer per function or per-fix file, readers after writers) and the gate is optimistic (speculative and batched runs, where a lost run costs only processor time).
Wait (lock or order) wherever a redo would waste tokens, and be optimistic only where the waste is processor time.
Dependencies are build order by default: level (1) OUT, CLAIM, CGATE, REDO, W1, W6, W7; (2) PLAN, W2, W5; (3) CLOSE, W3; (4) W4; largest first within a level.
Each of the 11 ordered and code points becomes a step function in its own per-fix file, not a stub in the shared file, so each file has one writer (the merge theorem covers only two edited regions).
The content points (B5, B8, B13, B14, B17, B18, B19, B20) are written in full by the skeleton, so a later change to them is a skeleton amendment.
Each ordered sequence is a fixed list of step functions in the FIX-JOIN order, each step in its owner's per-fix file (Calvin's idea applied by the skeleton).
A step that reads what another writes waits for the writer: W2 after W1, and W5 after W6, with their joint tests run at the later fix's gate.
The skeleton acts as the reconnaissance step for Calvin-style ordering, and the gate's footprint check is the recheck.
The same-statement points B8, B13 and B14 are written once by the skeleton writer with both fixes' content; each is one line or statement, checked by both fixes' tests.
The integration branch advances only if its tip is unchanged since the merge began (compare-and-swap, the gate's fencing token).
Ruled out: merging by a model 'by intent', testing every combination of waiting fixes, and a structured or semistructured merge tool.
Ruled out: real-time co-editing of one file with sequence CRDTs, because nothing in this case needs it.
Ruled out: who-talks-to-whom (socio-technical congruence) arguments for predicting conflicts.
Workflow C (one integrator per file group, merging by intent) is ruled out: its integrator is an unchecked transform function and its window grows with every patch.
Workflow A runs 7 fixes at once in level 1, then 3, 2 and 1; 13 at once only if step 9 allows stubs.
Workflow A's 15 agents carry about 900,000 tokens before any work (about 60,000 fixed each).
Workflow B's first level starts 4 fixes at once (OUT, CGATE, REDO, W6) once the WCP edges and W5 after W6 are kept.
Workflow A step 9: later levels start early on stubs only if p x R x (fixes started early) fits the remaining token allowance with margin; otherwise they wait (the default).
The speed-up over one builder is at most (T_w + 596) / 596 with single-run gating, and at most k times that with greedy batches of k that all pass.
If the USL coherency term b is near 0, the peak goes to infinity and the cap is Amdahl's 1/a (from the quoted USL paper, lit4 #9).
Gate capacity is T_w / 596 s builders with single runs, and k times that with passing batches of k; this caps the width.
Expected textual conflicts: Workflow A about 0 (unproven), Workflow B without layout up to 5 (B1, B5, B7, B17, B18), Workflow C 2.6 to 5.4.
Wasted work: Workflow A risks a rework per failed merge and a rebase per wrong signature; B risks idle slots; C throws away whatever the integrator cannot fit.
Agrawal's second condition for restarts (many transactions available) does not hold here, with 13 fixes.
Workflow A's time is T_0b + T_skel + 4 levels of T_w + gate tail, or one level fewer if step 9 allows stubs.
Per-fix files give a write-time check (the hook refuses a Write by path) and the gate refuses hunks outside the footprint.
CONTRACT decision 20 concerns the tree's run-time hook, not a build hook, so it does not conflict with the plan.
Designs held from the research tree: shared-nothing partitioning (SM D2-05) holds refined, optimistic control (SM D2-06) kept for the gate only, and one owner with read-only users (SM D8-08) kept.
No consensus, distributed locks or two-phase commit across sessions, and no speculative backup tasks, is consistent with the plan (SM do_not items).
The ruling 'One writer per file' (research-tree/RULINGS.md:33) is refined for building to one writer per function in shared files plus per-fix files, after the owner's rejection of 2026-11-18.
Thirteen fixes checked one by one through the gate take 13 x 596 s = 7,748 s (2 h 9 min), and 8,344 s with 0b added.
Not yet known: the time and tokens to write one fix (T_w, which 0b gives) and the failure rate p (which the first wave gives).
Symbols not measured: T_w (time to write one fix), T_skel (skeleton time), p (share of merges failing the suite), R (tokens per rework), T_r (rebase time).

Test 2, not run (about 20 min of processor, no model tokens): two suites side by side in two worktrees, then one suite with --test-concurrency=4; decides whether the gate can speculate or split a batch (floor about 270 s) and sets the retry rule.
Test 3, not run (one small Haiku session): a hook on Edit and Write inside a helper started with worktree isolation; decides whether files per builder are held at write time or only at the gate.
Test 4, not run: build 0b alone, recording T_w and tokens; sets gate capacity T_w / 596 s, the width cap and whether batching is worth building.

Test 5, not run: skeleton and level 1 logged for rebases, footprint refusals, failed merges (p), rework tokens (R) and wall-time speed-up at each width the window visits; sets batch size, whether later levels start on stubs, and the width.
Each of the five tests is an experiment under rule 3 and needs the owner's word before it runs.
Shell writes pass the write hook and are caught only at the gate; this is not tested.
Flaky tests: the rule for them is open; test 2's base runs would add flake data at no extra cost.
A builder's peak memory is not measured; the width cap needs it (SM D3-03).
The signatures the skeleton must fix are not yet listed.
CONTRACT decision 19 ('what two scripts share is in lib') is to be checked against the contract text when the skeleton is written.
The USL coherency term b, the peak and where adding builders turns retrograde cannot be computed; with at most 13 builders a fit from 2 or 3 widths must not be extrapolated.
